1 Introduction

This document provides a practical catalogue of specialist systems by industry, with representative providers. It is intended as a reference for enterprise architecture, IT strategy, operating model design, digital transformation, and industry capability mapping.

The catalogue is structured using the following fields:

  • Industry
  • Specialist Capability
  • System Type
  • Purpose
  • Typical Providers

This is not an exhaustive market analysis. Provider names are illustrative and represent common or well-known vendors in each category.

2 How to Use This Catalogue

This reference can support several use cases:

  • enterprise architecture inventories
  • target operating model design
  • application portfolio assessments
  • industry capability mapping
  • vendor landscape overviews
  • digital transformation discovery work
  • PMO and IT governance documentation

A useful extension is to add fields such as:

  • business owner
  • technical owner
  • deployment model
  • integration points
  • criticality
  • regulatory relevance
  • data classification
  • lifecycle status

4 Cross-Industry Observations

Although these systems are industry-specific, they usually fall into a smaller number of architectural categories.

4.1 Operational Control Systems

These directly control or monitor operations, often in real time.

Examples include:

  • SCADA
  • DCS
  • EMS
  • ADMS
  • OSS
  • fleet dispatch systems

4.2 Core Transaction Systems

These execute the primary business transactions of an industry.

Examples include:

  • core banking
  • policy administration
  • PSS
  • PMS
  • SIS
  • POS

4.3 Record and Compliance Systems

These provide legally or operationally important records.

Examples include:

  • EHR
  • PACS
  • LIS
  • CTMS
  • RMS
  • case management systems

4.4 Planning and Execution Systems

These support operational planning, workflow, and optimisation.

Examples include:

  • WMS
  • TMS
  • MES
  • project controls systems
  • mine planning systems
  • farm management systems

7 Architecture Notes

7.1 Specialist Systems Are Usually Not Standalone

Most specialist systems are heavily integrated with broader enterprise platforms such as:

  • ERP
  • CRM
  • identity and access management
  • data warehouse / data lake
  • integration middleware
  • reporting and analytics platforms
  • document management systems
  • monitoring and cyber security tooling

7.2 Industry Systems Often Drive Core Value Creation

In many industries, the specialist system is the operational core. For example:

  • a bank depends on core banking
  • an airline depends on its PSS
  • a hospital depends on EHR and PACS
  • a utility depends on ADMS/OMS/CIS
  • a factory depends on SCADA, DCS, and MES

7.3 Governance Considerations

When cataloguing specialist systems, it is useful to assess them through several lenses:

  • business criticality
  • resilience requirements
  • information security
  • compliance and regulation
  • vendor lock-in risk
  • integration complexity
  • data ownership
  • lifecycle and technical debt

8 Practical Use in IT Strategy

This catalogue can support strategic analysis such as:

8.1 Application Portfolio Review

Identify:

  • duplicate systems
  • unsupported legacy systems
  • strategic systems
  • systems needing modernisation
  • cyber and resilience priorities

8.2 Capability Mapping

Map applications to business capabilities and determine:

  • which capabilities are well supported
  • which depend on manual processes
  • where transformation investment is needed

8.3 Target Architecture Design

Use the catalogue to define:

  • strategic platforms
  • integration principles
  • data ownership
  • coexistence between legacy and modern platforms

9 Conclusion

Specialist systems vary by industry, but the design logic is similar across sectors. Every industry tends to rely on a combination of:

  • operational control systems
  • core transaction systems
  • record and compliance systems
  • planning and execution systems

A structured catalogue helps organisations understand where these systems sit in the enterprise landscape, how they support business capabilities, and where they create operational dependency, risk, and strategic value.
